The Trans-New Guinea (TNG) language family is the largest language family spread within the linguistically diverse island of New Guinea [@pawley2017; @bellwood2001]. Where, when, why, and how the TNG language family spread across the breadth of New Guinea, and into neighboring islands, is a topic of ongoing discussion, but current evidence point to the advent of agriculture in the Wahgi valley, starting around 10kya, resulting in population growth, followed by the expansion of people, and spread and divergence languages from a common source [@bergström2017, @denham2003, @shaw2020, @schapper2017]. The demographic spread of a language family is termed demic-diffusion [@guglielmino1995]. A theoretical alternative to demic-diffusion is the cultural spread of language without the rise and dispersal of a founding population, called cultural diffusion, where groups of people change language without any significant change in the gene pool [@guglielmino1995; @padilla-iglesias2024]. The complexity of human history is such that multiple diffusion models are likely at play in the spread of any language family, and this would be particularly true for an area of such extreme diversity as New Guinea. Various disciplines have attempted to discern the relative importance of the demic and cultural processes within New Guinea [@schapper2017, @denham2003], and other agriculturally-driven expansions [@diamond2003, @mccoll2018,], but the test of a demic-diffusion model demands an interdisciplinary approach.

For a correlation between linguistic and genetic diversity to persist under a model of demic-diffusion, languages must be repeatedly transmitted from parent to child, just like how genes are inherited [@gray2010, @labov2007]. Linguistic reconstruction is thought to have a much shallower time-depth than genetics, perhaps to a maximal depth of 8k years, due to the rate at which language changes [@nichols1992]. However, while the reconstruction of language features may be limited, the channels of language can plausibly persist for longer, allowing a deeper view of the linguistic past, despite not being able to identify features of languages [@lansing2017; @sapir1949]. This paper is looking for language channels linked to a Trans-New Guinea demic-expansion within a genetic sample that includes speakers of TNG and non-TNG languages [@attenborough2010].

### Existing evidence for the spread of TNG

The developing story of the origin of TNG points to an origin in the Waghi Valley of the East New Guinea highlands. This is the home to groups of TNG languages that show the deepest and most robust linguistic history[^1] [@pawley2005; @schapper2017], with archaeological evidence suggesting the early stages of agriculture began in the Kuk Swamp (within the Waghi valley) around 10kya, with agricultural advancements apparent at 6kya, and 4kya [@denham2003, @shaw2020]. The invention of agriculture elsewhere in the world has often correlated with a spread of languages [@diamond2003, @haak2015], creating geographically dispersed and linguistically diverse family, as well as global patterns of linguistic and genetic diversity showing strong relationships [@creanza2015, @cavalli-sforza1991], seemingly mediated by kinship systems [@pichkar2024]. It is the coincidence of linguistic origins and the archeaological evidence of agriculture in the East New Guinea Highlands that points to the hypothesis that TNG spread through demographic growth and spread around 10kya.

[^1]: Although, it is worth pointing out that the family as a whole is largely a hypothesis, and evidence for establishing the breadth and depth of the languages involved is not from universally agreed.

The existing genetic evidence for a TNG expansion leans towards a model of demic-diffusion from the Wahgi valley after the adoption of agriculture. As far as we can see, there has be no direct test of the demic-diffusion of TNG within the genetic literature, but there have been some indirect tests. The most informative of those showed that when genetic populations were defined by language families 15 TNG to TNG family comparisons showed no genetic differentiation (19% of all comparisons), 9 TNG to non-TNG comparisons showed no genetic differentiation (12%), but all comparisons between non-TNG populations were genetically distinct [@harley2006]. While this is suggestive of an demic-expansion of TNG, as well as integrating the expanding population with Indigenous groups, the author suggests caution in this conclusion, pointing to the confound of geographic distance [@attenborough2010]. Less direct tests highlight genetic distinctions between areas we know are linguistically distinct, although these papers do not explicitly test this. @bergström2017 identify a distinct genetic pattern between New Guinea Highland and lowland populations, showing effective population sizes take off in Southern Highlands, Chimbu, and Madang, around 10,000 years ago. @mona2007 identify two genetic haplogroups (K-M254 and M-P34) in North-West New Guinea that have suggested origins in the New Guinea, Highlands around 6kya found amongst speakers of TNG languages.

The genetic divergence between Highland and Lowlanders is mediated by several genetic admixture events, suggesting frequent contact between the purported home of TNG and other areas [@brucato2021], possibly aided by ubiquitous multilingualism and sister-exchange marriage practices [@evans2012]. The culturally-perpetuated disease *kuru* disrupted the co-evolution of genes and language in some regions, which, during 1958-59, resulted in the death of a significant portion of women in Fore-speaking communities of the Eastern Highlands, and their surrounds [@quinn2024; @liu2020]. Communities with high female mortality were then required to reach beyond existing wife-exchange networks to continue to reproduce, which possibly disrupted the correlation between linguistic and genetic diversity that existed outside the communities affected by Kuru [@li2020].

Linguistic evidence cannot speak directly to a demic-diffusion model, but in general research connecting TNG expansion to agriculture is limited [@schapper2017]. Linguistic reconstruction for the words of key crops such as taro, sugarcane, and bananas provide weak evidence to a common source of agricultural traditions for TNG speakers [@schapper2017; @pawley2017], but further comparisons are limited without more detailed linguistic documentation, which is often hard-fought to obtain and increasingly scarce due to the rise of language endangerment [@bromham2022a]. Nevertheless, historical linguistic research tells us that the TNG family has spread far, connecting languages as far west as Timor Leste to the Trans-New Guinea family, as far east as Milne Bay, and with sub-families covering the Central Corridella and covers much of the southern parts of New Guinea Island [@pawley2017, @usher2022].

In this paper, we use mtDNA samples taken across Papua New Guinea, alongside linguistic metadata detailing the primary languages of individuals, and the languages of their parents, to test the hypothesis that linguistic expansion of TNG languages was primarily the result of a demographic expansion. Because the start of this expansion is older than what we can reconstruct language history, and because we are testing the assumption that the underlying cause was demographic, we are testing whether the persistent parent-child transmission of TNG languages has left a language channel in the genetic data. If there is a langauge channel in the genetic data, we should expect that TNG speakers are more likely to cluster together than speakers of other languages, and what the time-depth of that cluster is [@attenborough2010]. This is done by first building a mitochondrial phylogeny of 356 individuals across New Guinea (Figure @fig-TNGtree; @lansing2017). Then, using their linguistic metadata, we identify those who speak either a language from within TNG, or one of 12 other sampled families, calculating the probability that genetically related individuals share a language trait every 25 years over the life of the phylogeny.

An important point to immediately address is the use of linguistic data which is more likely to be paternally inherited due to the prevalence of patrilocal residence across New Guinea, against a genetic phylogeny that is maternally inherited. Ideally, this paper would examine the patterns across both mtDNA and Non-recombinant Y phylogeny (as in @lansing2017), but data from male line was not as readily available. Despite the assumption that the prevalence of patrilocality would muddle the gene-language correlation, 86% of parents in our sample speak the same language (n = 154), and 98% of TNG speakers parents speak languages from the same sub-family of TNG. This pattern is suggestive of language family endogamy, and that mtDNA can maintain the signal of a language channel, particularly when looking at higher level linguistic categories.

We find evidence for gene-language correlation in TNG until around 20k years ago. This correlation is not present across all TNG groups however, being primarily driven by a stronger gene-language relationship in Kainantu-Goroka and Angan speakers. The temporal correlation suggests that demic-diffusion was a plausible cause for the spread of Trans-New Guinea languages, but linguistic channels of inheritance were likely to have existed prior to the advent of agriculture and that some sub-families had disproportionate influence on the spread of TNG. Future work should examine what social conditions might cause a differential in demographic spread, how different sub-families persisted in the presence of an expansive neighbors, and the relative importance of the demic-diffusion model against a cultural diffusion model.

# Materials

## Samples and Ethics

We use `r n_samples` existing mtDNA samples in this study (See Table SX for details). In all cases, participants completed a questionnaire to determine language affiliation(s), current residence, date and place of birth, and a short genealogy of up to two generations to establish regional ancestry. Only individuals with a full regional ancestry over at least two generations were sampled (see @andré2021 for details). Samples were restricted those taken from mainland New Guinea, and were not associated with the Austronesian expansion (i.e. individuals with a B4a1 haplogroup).

For samples in @andré2021, complete mtDNA sequences were extracted from whole genome sequences generated at CNRGH, France. Sequencing libraries were prepared using Tru-Seq DNA PCR-Free and TruSeq Nano DNA HT kits depending on DNA quantity. See the original publications for the sequencing procedure of all other samples. For all samples, consensus sequences were obtained after base-calling, quality filtering, and further quality control steps to obtain consensus sequences, as described previously [@arias2018].

### Linguistic Metadata

All individuals provided information on their primary language. 212 individuals speak Trans-New Guinea Languages, and 109 speak languages from other families. The 212 TNG speakers are split across 10 different sub-families, from a total of 39 sub-families \[Evans&Fedden forthcoming\] . The majority speak Kainantu-Goroka languages (number of genetic samples = 88), followed by Chimbu-Wahgi languages (49), Angan (41), Enga-Kewa-Huli (18), Suki-Gogodala (5), Kiwaian (5), Madang (2), Wiru (2), Ok-Oksapmin (1), and Mailuan (1). The classifications of languages within TNG is not universally agreed, however, all these sub-families are currently uncontroversial in their status as TNG language clades [@greenhill, @dryer2022].

Of the 109 non-TNG speakers, 22 individuals listed a primary language from the Bosavi family; 19 speakers speak Pahoturi langauges, 14 Yam speakers; eight speakers of Arafundi langauges; six Suki-Gogodala speakers; five Lower-Sepik speakers; three Ndu speakers, two speakers of the isolate langauge, Wiru \[wiu\], and one speaker from each of the Sepik (Kwoma \[kmo\]), Eleman (Orokolo \[oro\]), and South Bougainville (Siwai \[siw\]) families. These speakers cover 10 of around \~40 Papuan language families found across New Guinea. 17 individuals listed Tok Pisin as their primary language, a Pacific Creole and state recognized languages of PNG. Tok Pisin is known to have spread recently in PNG and beyond [@meakins2023], so this language is treated as missing data. The majority of these individuals offered linguistic data on their parents languages, which were not Tok Pisin, so their genetic information is retained in the phylogeny. 11 individuals listed Austronesian languages as their primary language, despite showing Papuan ancestry. These are examples of language shift, where individuals from a genetic lineage speak a language that we know did not expand alongside it. Language shift is pervasive between Papuan and Austronesian languages and is well documented in New Guinea and across the Pacific [@lipson2020, @lipson2018, @posth2018]. Nine of the 11 Austronesian speakers were sampled from the south-east tip of PNG, across the Oro, Central, National Capital, Morobe, and Milne Bay provinces.

To test the linguistic structure of genetic diversity in the phylogeny we create six linguistic variables. The first is whether the primary language of an individual in within TNG (1) or not (0). This variable will be used to determine if there is a distinct genetic signal between the theorized demic expansion of TNG speakers and other language families [@attenborough2010]. As stated above, it is unlikely the same process applies across the diversity of TNG, so the second and third variables test the structuring of genetic diversity against sub-families of TNG, and then at the language level. By increasing the specificity of our analysis, we can look at the linguistic-gene co-evolution across a range of linguistic scales. In our sample of 139 individuals who report both paternal and maternal languages, 125 parental couples speak languages from the same family, and 113 parents are reported as speaking the same language. Making the fourth, fifth, sixth, and 7th variables repetitions of the previous variables, but for the language spoken by an individuals father (n = 145), or mother (n = 143).

# Methods

## Phylogeny

The phylogeny is built using BEAST v2.7.4 [@bouckaert2019]\]. The substitution model is estimated using the package bModeltest to assess the most appropriate Substitution model [@bouckaert2017]. bModeltest will switch between all transition and transversion models, providing the model average across the runs and means we do not need to commit to a particular substitution model.

The phylogeny uses a Coalescent Extended Bayesian Skyline Population history model (EBSP). The EBSP model leverages coalescent theory to account for fluctuating population size in the phylogenetic model [@heled2008]. The sparsity of historical knowledge in Southern New Guinea means we do not have a good understanding of historic changes in population size. We opt for using a model that will allow for a fluctuating population, rather than assuming that it did not fluctuate. We adjust the factor rate of the tree prior to 0.5, and change the population prior mean to an improper prior of 1/x, as suggested in @heled2008. Mutation rates are estimated using an optimized relaxed clock, with a mean rate of of 2.4065 x 10^-8^ [@douglas2021]. This is derived by taking the mean value from studies calibrating the human mitochondrial clock [@rieux2014; @fu2013]. The phylogeny also contains tiered monophyletic groupings for the M and N haplogroups, and then for M2, N13, P3, and Q haplogroups. The MCMC chain was run for 100,000,000 iterations, sampling every 5,000, with a 30% burn-in period. All parameters showed effective samples sizes greater than 200.

## Estimating the heritage of traits

To estimate the 'channels of language', we calculate the probability of two individuals sharing a language within a genetic clade, across the phylogenetic history. This calculation follows from @lansing2017 and comes in the form:

$$
P(i_l,j_l)|i_{g(t)}, j_{g(t)}) = \frac{P(i_l, j_l \bigcap i_{g(t)}, j_{g(t)})}{P(i_{g(t)}, j_{g(t)}} = \frac{\sum_{g=1}^{c_t}(\sum_{i,j\neq i}1_{cos(l_ig, l_jg) > 0})}{\sum_{g=1}^{c_t}n_g(n_g - 1) / 2}
$$

$c_t$ is the number of genetic clades at any point in history, for t generations. We assume 25 year generation times. $l_{i_g}$ and $l_{j_g}$ are the languages or language families spoken by individuals within genetic clade $g$. $1_{cos(l_{i_g}, l_{i_g}) > 0}$ is an indicator function, returning 1 if the *ith* and *jth* individual share a language, and zero otherwise. $n_g$ is the number of individuals in $g$. We perform this calculation across a random posterior of 5,000 trees. Expanding on @lansing2017, we compare the posterior probability calculation to a permuted trait across the posterior. The permuted trait shows the probability of sharing a language with a genetically related individual if languages were distributed randomly, which is also combined with our uncertainty in the phylogenetic posterior.

Data and code for this analysis can be found at XXX. Functions for calculating the phylogenetic heritage of traits are held in the package `traitheritage`, which can be found at `github.com/SamPassmore/traitheritage`.

# Results

## Haplogroups

The majority of TNG speakers have a P1d (30%) or Q1 haplogroup (28%), which are also the most frequent haplogroups amongst non-TNG speakers (P1d = 17%; Q1 = 21%; Table @tbl-haplogroups). Speakers of TNG languages then show decreasing frequency of haplogroups Q1a (12%), P2 (8%), P1 (6%); P4 (6%), Q3 (4%), and minor proportions (\<4%) of M, N, N13, P, P3, P3b1, Q1d, and Q2. As stated Q1 is the most common haplogroup among non-TNG speakers followed by P1d, and in decreasing order Q3 (10%), N13 (8%), P3 (7%), P2 (7%), P4 (5%), and minor proportions (\<4%) of M, P3b1, E, S2, and P haplogroups. The largest difference in proportions between these two groups is the rate of P1d, which 13% more frequent among TNG speakers than non-TNG, despite being common among both linguistic categories, which is significant statistical difference ($\chi^2 = 5.36, p = 0.02$) . Q1 is also proportionally higher (6%) among TNG speakers, which is also one of the most frequent haplogroups for non-TNG speakers, but this is not a significant difference ($\chi^2 = 1.18, p = 0.28$). N13 (8% higher), P3 (6%), and Q3 (6%) are all haplogroups that are proportionally higher in Non-TNG groups. These proportions point to some vague affiliations of P1d haplogroups with TNG, but are by no means definitive. Treating non-TNG as a homogeneous category for comparison is misleading because of the diversity of linguistic lineages it contains, so we make no conclusions on defining non-TNG haplogroups.

## Phylogeny

From BEAST, a posterior of 10,000(check) phylogeny were extracted, which contain support for existing models of genetic diversification in New Guinea [@purnomo2021; @pedro2020; Figure @fig-TNGtree]. The Maximum Clade Credibility (MCCT) phylogeny is dated to 71kya (95% HPD: 58k - 84k). The haplogroups P1d and Q1, which contain the highest proportion of TNG speakers, are dated to 33k (26k - 40k; approximately the same as @pedro2020), and 27k (22k - 33k; around 10k younger than is found in @pedro2020 and @purnomo2021). These dates make it likely these haplogroups arose before the expansion of TNG. N13, P3, and Q3, haplogroups proportionally more common among non-TNG speakers show deeper time depths of 56k (45k - 66k), 51k (42k - 59k), and 40k (33k - 48k), respectively.

```{r TNG}

Each taxa is labelled with whether an individual speaks a TNG language (red) or not (yellow). The RHS graph shows the probability of a shared language within a genetic clade over time (red), and the posterior variance of this calculation (light red). A a baseline null hypothesis, we also show the same calculation with randomly permuted tips (blue). We permute the tip 30 times for each of the 10,000 trees. The light green error bands contain both the phylogenetic error, and permutation error."
#| cap-location: bottom
```

### Language affiliation structures genetic history better than chance

TNG speaking individuals shows a strong genetic clustering when compared to the random permutation of languages, up to around 20kya (Figure @fig-TNGtree). From 3,745 years onwards the 95% High Density Intervals (HDI) show no overlap between the true data and the permuted data, suggesting that affiliation to TNG languages structures genetic diversity better than chance. The depth of the separation persists strongly until just before 20kya, but is weakly distinct (\<1% different) until 50kya. The most recent 3,745 years show highly variable probability results, with wide-errors. This is because there are few genetic coalescent events before this time (relative to the total number in the tree), meaning the probabilities fluctuate with each new bifurcation, and therefore the permutations also show high error.

This result provides evidence that TNG affiliation structures genetic diversity, but assuming that all TNG groups diversified through the same process is naïve. We break down the probabilities of the above graph by the major branches of TNG, to examine their relative influence to the gene-language correlation. Because there are less possible pairs now, we see a reduction of overall probability, but in return there is a more detailed view of the gene-language correlation.

Across our sample, there is sufficient data (\>5 genetic samples) to examine the gene-language correlation in seven non-TNG language families (90 individuals), and six TNG sub-families (267; Figure @fig-byfamily; note that this graph is restricted to 30kya, focusing on the significant period in Figure @fig-TNGtree). In general, TNG sub-families (red) have stronger links to genetic history than non-TNG languages (yellow). Non-TNG families were analysed separately, but their cumulatively low gene-language correlation meant they were aggregated for aesthetic reasons. The gene-language correlation is strongest among Kainantu-Goroka speakers, followed by Chimbu-Wahgi, and then Angan. Notably, there are more samples from within TNG than outside it, and the TNG sub-families with the largest samples also show the strongest signal. To assess whether the correlation reflects more than the frequency of samples, the results are compared to a permutation result. Angan, Chimbu-Wahgi, and Kainantu-Goroka populations show a significant difference, which suggests the effect is robust to sample size. Amongst Angan speakers, the signal is weak with linguistic signal begining in the genetic data at `r angan_timedepth[1,2]` years and running until `r angan_timedepth[2,2]` years. More data might reveal a stronger relationship. Within Chimbu-Wahgi speakers, the signal starts around `r cw_timedepth[2,1]` until `r cw_timedepth[2,2]`. Amongst speakers of Kainantu-Goroka languages, the signal starts earlier, at `r kaingor_timedepth[1,2]` years, and also runs slightly later to `r kaingor_timedepth[2,2]` years ago.

# Geographic confounding weakens the causal gene-language relationship

A confounding variable in the correlation of genes and languages is geography [@sokal1988]. That is, since genetic similarity and linguistic similarity both decay as distance between point increases, it is possible that the observed correlation is a caused by the constraints of geography and not because of a causal relationship between the spread of people and language. The confounding influence of geography can be circumvented through a quasi-experimental approach, and examining the correlation for individuals who are genetically and linguistically close, but geographically distant.

Here, we test that possibility by calculating the probability of shared genetic history given a shared language, as before, as well as the pair of individuals homelands being within or beyond a walking time of 12, 24, or 48 hours as determined by Tobler's hiking distance [@tobler1993]. Note that this is continuous walking time, so 48 hours of walking would take 4 to 5 days if walking approximately 10 hours per day. Each pair of individuals falls into one of four categories: a pair of individuals share a language, and are close by (L & D); they share a language but are not close by (L & ¬D); they are close by but do not share a language (¬L & D), or they do not share a language and are not close by (¬L & ¬D). Categorizing pairs in this way is an attempt to observe the language-gene correlation without the confound of geography, but as a simple binary measure, fails to accurately represent the historical movement of people - since it assumes that contemporary locations remain the same over time. Nevertheless, it is an improvement on ignoring the problem. Probability is calculated in the same way as discussed above, recording the probability of each paired category at each 25 year time-step (Figure @fig-distance).

Proportionally, most people are both close to each other and either both speak or both do not speak a TNG language (37% of pairs are within 48hr walk and share a linguistic history, Figure @fig-distance). 35% of individuals are both more than 48hr walk away, and do not share a linguistic history, while only 24% of individuals share a linguistic history but are not geographically close.

Since we are only interested in whether geography is a confounding factor in the correlation between genes and languages in the spread of TNG, we can focus on whether genetically related pairs share a language and are not close by (L & ¬D). If this category shows a significant difference to a permuted result, the inference is that people and languages are moving together, and they are moving further than a 48 hour walk, suggestive of an expansive population and in line with the geographically expansive linguistic history of TNG [@usher2022].

A comparison of the genetic pairs with shared linguistic history, and geographic separation at 12hrs, 24hrs, and 48hr walking distance shows no difference to a permuted test. This means we cannot rule out the possibility that genetic and linguistic diversification of Trans-New Guinea languages occurred at different times with this statistical approach.

```{r distance_exp}
## Summarise Permutations
sum_perm = function(df){
  df %>% 
    mutate(generation =  as.numeric(gsub("g_", replacement = "", generation))) %>% 
      filter(generation < 50000) %>% 
      mutate(posterior = rep(1:51, each = (2000 * 5))) %>% 
      group_by(generation, posterior) %>%
      summarise(wntree_cladeprob = mean(p_lang_nodist, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% 
      ungroup() %>% 
      group_by(generation) %>% 
      summarise(p_lang_nodist_probability = mean(wntree_cladeprob, na.rm = TRUE),
                ci_hdi = bayestestR::ci(wntree_cladeprob)) %>% 
      ungroup() %>% 
      tidyr::unpack(ci_hdi)  
}
```

# Discussion

This study has shown a correlation between mtDNA and language amongst TNG speaking individuals, up to a date of around 20kya. Examining the correlation more closely, we observe the correlation is not heterogenous across sub-families of TNG. Chimbu-Wahgi, Kainantu-Goroka, and possibly Angan speakers appear to be the driving the gene-language correlation within TNG. Each of these families show a strong link up to around 12kya. However, a confounding variable in the gene-langauge correlation is geographic proximity. A quasi-experimental approach showed us that it was not possible with the given sample to rule out the possibility that the correlation is due to incidental spread of genes and language over distance, and not because of a causal relationship between the two.

The time-depth of the gene-language correlation within the TNG family is deeper than what archaeological evidence currently suggests. That being the evidence for agriculture developing in the Wahgi valley at 10kya at the latest. These results are not in conflict, since the advent of agriculture does not signal the beginning of a population, only when we might expect to see an increase in the population size. Depending on the position of first arrival, simulations of the peopling of Sahul point arrival dates around the central corridella between 30 and 24kya (depending on the inclusion or exclusion of Madjedbebe; @bradshaw2021), or around 4 to 6kya after the arrival of humans [@bradshaw2023]. Genetic evidence also highlights the migration of populations in a similar area between 50 to 20kya [@brucato2021], within distinct population divide between highlanders and lowlanders arising between 10-20kya [@bergström2017]. We tentatively suggest the results in this paper suggest the existing populations were likely to be linguistically homogenous groups. Further tests of this hypothesis could use population phylogenetic comparative techniques developed in @barbieri2022, and using the recently developed TNG linguistic phylogeny [@greenhill].

The varying correlation strength across sub-families of TNG is a novel finding, showing that Angan and Kainantu-Goroka have strong gene-language correlations. Specifically, these language families have strong internal correlations, which might reflect a preference for language-family endogamy (marrying people from groups who speak similar languages), or perhaps more likely, a strong geographic constraint on where marriage partners can come from. Testing whether these language family connections are found across the genome (i.e. are not just found in the mtDNA), and whether they are also robust to geographic confounds is a promising avenue for future work. It is also likely that some of the higher-level correlation is driven by strong patterns of exchange between TNG sub-families, which would align with the history of exogamous exchange patterns observed in the highlands [@li2020, @weiner1982], but importantly not with non-TNG groups. The lack of correlation between genes and language is an interesting finding, although not the focus of this study. The prevalence of sister-exchange and longstanding connections across language boundaries is a well attested feature of New Guinea kinship [@evans2012, @busse1987, @williams1936]. The history of this practice could feasibly resulted in a pan-mixed population. Without a more direct test, alongside a detailed understanding of the marriage and residence patterns, may reveal the interwoven histories of non-TNG groups in future work.

The evidence for the demic-diffusion of TNG languages alongside the spread of mtDNA is founded upon layers of statistical approximation. Statistical models come with assumptions that need to laid out for the fair evaluation of the results. Firstly, the permutations of languages is a weak null hypothesis because we know a-priori that both languages and genes are spatially, not randomly, distributed [@guglielmino1995, @cavalli-sforza1991]. We have attempted to parse out the influence of geography through a quasi-experimental approach, but find that the gene-language relationship is not stronger than the random permutation of languages. This is not necessarily because there is no relationship, but more likely because the genetic sample is densely clustered within Papua New Guinea. TNG as a whole contains between 100 and 400 languages (depending on the TNG classification used [@pawley2017]), as well as stretching from Timor-Leste to Milne. With a sample that contains more geographic breadth, alongside a more complex model of how the influence of geography might change over time, it is feasible to parse out the causal relationship between the spread of genes and language in the spread of TNG.

Secondly, mtDNA only contains the history of one gene with specific maternal properties. As noted earlier, paternally inherited genes might are likely more informative in the spread of TNG because of the prevalence of patrilineal descent [@lansing2017, @barbieri2013]. Population genetic approach also provide a fruitful avenue for a more detailed view of the genetic picture. For example, examination of Bantu expansion and interactions with Central African Hunting groups (CAHG) use SNPs and masking technique to identify to identify Bantu introgression in CAGH and identify timings of cultural change in the CAGH [@padilla-iglesias2024]. New Guinea contains many environments of an expanding population into a populated region where these methods might be applicable. Most notable is the expansion of TNG into South New Guinea, home to four other existing language families that might pre-date the arrival of TNG.

Finally, our methodological approach is estimating probabilities based on a phylogenetic model. It is important to be cautious when interpreting results based on models of the past, because of the compounding error. Here, we taken a conservative approach incorporating phylogenetic and posterior error, but it is important to consider the simplifications of human history that are made under a phylogenetic model. Phylogenies are abstract representation of history, reflecting assumptions about the mechanisms (e.g. groups can only bifurcate) and rates of change (e.g. are rates constant or variable across branches in the tree? are mtDNA mutation rates similar across different geographies of human history?) and are subject to interpretation [@bromham2022]. Here, we model the channels of language on-top of a historical abstraction. This allows principled tests on the hypothesis of the role of genes in the spread of languages, and allows us to quantify the role of confounding variables (like geography) on our conclusions, but it is a further step on the abstraction of the past meaning this study should be considered a small piece of evidence towards the demic-diffusion of TNG, but not a foundational piece of evidence.

# Conclusion

This paper has used and developed some new approaches to combining linguistics and genetics to uncover their intersecting histories in the context of TNG languages. Having showed that TNG speakers seem to share a genetic history up to around 20kya with existing methods, we offer new approaches to soften the causal validity of this finding, suggesting that geographic constraints are a likely confounding factor in the correlation. Future work could use the same methods with a more geographically dispersed sampled, to circumvent the confounding of geography, or explore more complicated quasi-experimental approaches to parse out the influence of genetic versus geographic spread of the TNG family.
